exampleAnswers.title: Describing Properties of the Cotangent Function

question.text:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the function $y=\cot x?$ Assume $n$ is an integer.

  1. The domain of the function is $(-\infty, +\infty).$
  2. $\cot(x)= \cot(x-\pi)$
  3. The function has a vertical asymptote at $x=-5\pi.$
question.explanation:
Let's plot the graph of $y=\cot x.$

Now, let's go through each statement.

  • Statement I is false. The domain of the function is all the real numbers except for the points $x=n\pi.$

  • Statement II is true. Since the period of $\cot x$ is $\pi$, we have $\cot(x + n\pi) = \cot x$ for any integer $n.$ Thus, for $n=-1,$ we get $\cot(x)=\cot(x-\pi).$

  • Statement III is true. The lines $x=n\pi$ are the vertical asymptotes of the function. Thus, $x=-5\pi$ is a vertical asymptote.

question.text:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the function $y=\cot x?$

  1. The function has a vertical asymptote at $x=11\pi.$
  2. The range of the function is $\left( -\infty, \infty \right).$
  3. $x=-\dfrac{3\pi}{2}$ is a root of the function.
question.explanation:
Let's plot the graph of $y=\cot x.$

Now, let's go through each statement.

  • Statement I is true. The vertical asymptotes of the function are at integer multiples of $\pi$, i.e., $x=n\pi,$ where $n$ is any integer.

  • Statement II is true. The range of $y=\cot x$ is $(-\infty, \infty).$

  • Statement III is true. The zeros of $y=\cot{x}$ occur at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}+n\pi,$ for any integer $n.$ Therefore, $x=-\dfrac{3\pi}{2}$ is a root of the function.

exampleAnswers.title: Utilizing the Periodicity Property of the Cotangent Function

question.text: If $\cot x = 4$ for some $x$, then find the value of $\dfrac 1 2\cot(x+2\pi)-3 .$
question.explanation:
The period of $y = \cot x$ is $\pi.$ Therefore, for integer $n$ we have

\[ \cot{x} = \cot{(x+n\pi)} . \]

Substituting $n=2$ into the right-hand-side of the above gives

\begin{align*} \cot{x} = \cot{(x+(2)\cdot\pi)} = \cot(x+2\pi) . \end{align*}

Therefore, if $\cot{x} = 4,$ then $\cot{(x+2\pi)} = 4.$

Finally, then

\begin{align} \dfrac 1 2\cot(x+2\pi)-3 &= \dfrac 1 2 (4) - 3\\[5pt] &= 2-3 \\[5pt] &= -1 . \end{align}

question.text: If $\cot x = -4$ for some $x,$ then find the value of $3\cot(x+17\pi)+6.$
question.explanation:
The period of $y = \cot x$ is $\pi.$ Therefore, for any integer $n,$ we have

\[ \cot{x} = \cot{(x+n\pi)}. \]

Substituting $n=17$ into the above gives

\begin{align*} \cot{x} &= \cot{(x+17\cdot\pi)} \\[3pt] &= \cot(x+17\pi). \end{align*}

Therefore, if $\cot{x} = -4,$ then $\cot{(x+17\pi)} = -4.$

Finally, then

\begin{align*} 3\cot(x+7\pi)+6 &= 3 (-4) + 6 \\[3pt] &= -12+6 \\[3pt] &= -6. \end{align*}

exampleAnswers.title: Utilizing the Oddness Property of the Cotangent Function

question.explanation:
First, let's recall the graph of $y=\cot{x}.$

From the graph, we note the following:

  • The period of $\cot{x}$ is $\pi.$

  • Our graph has rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin. This means that $\cot{x}$ is an odd function, and we have \[ \cot(-x) = -\cot{x}. \]

Let's now evaluate our expression:

  • Firstly, using the periodicity of $\cot{x},$ we have \begin{align} \cot(-x+15\pi) &= \cot(-x + \pi \cdot 15) \\[3pt] &= \cot(-x). \end{align}

  • Secondly, using the oddness of $\cot{x},$ we have \begin{align} \cot(-x) &= -\cot{x} \\[5pt] &= -\left(-6\right) \\[5pt] &= 6. \end{align}

Therefore,

\begin{align} \dfrac{1}{2}\cot (-x+15\pi)+7 &= \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot 6 + 7 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{6}{2} + 7 \\[5pt] &= 3 + 7 \\[5pt] &= 10. \end{align}

example.title: Utilizing the Oddness Property of the Cotangent Function

question.explanation:
First, let's recall the graph of $y=\cot{x}.$

From the graph, we note the following:

  • The period of $\cot{x}$ is $\pi.$

  • Our graph has rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin. This means that $\cot{x}$ is an odd function, and we have \[ \cot(-x) = -\cot{x}. \]

Let's now evaluate our expression:

  • Firstly, using the periodicity of $\cot{x},$ we have \begin{align} \cot(-x+9\pi) &= \cot(-x + \pi \cdot 9) \\[3pt] &= \cot(-x). \end{align}

  • Secondly, using the oddness of $\cot{x},$ we have \begin{align} \cot(-x) &= -\cot{x} \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{3}{10}. \end{align}

Therefore,

\begin{align} 5\cot (-x+9\pi)-\dfrac{1}{2} &= 5\cdot \left(-\dfrac{3}{10}\right) - \dfrac{1}{2} \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{15}{10} - \dfrac{1}{2} \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{3}{2} -\dfrac{1}{2} \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{4}{2} \\[5pt] &= -2. \end{align}

From the graph, we note the following:

example.title: Utilizing the Oddness Property of the Cotangent Function

question.explanation:
First, let's recall the graph of $y=\cot{x}.$

Our graph has rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin. If we rotate the graph $180^\circ$ around the origin, we get the same picture. This means that $\cot{x}$ is an odd function, and we have \[ \cot(-x) = -\cot{x}. \]

Therefore,

\begin{align*} \cot(-x) &= - \cot{x} \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{5}{2}. \end{align*}
